description: How unemployment is measured, its main types and causes, and the effects on individuals, firms and the economy.
content_html:
What Do We Mean by Employment and Unemployment?

When economists talk about employment, they mean people who are in paid work. Unemployment refers to people who are without a job but are actively looking for one. These two concepts are central to understanding how well an economy is performing. When unemployment rises, it signals that the economy is not generating enough work for its people — output is lost, incomes fall, and government spending on benefits increases.

Not everyone without a job counts as unemployed. People who are retired, studying full-time, caring for family members, or who have stopped looking for work are described as economically inactive. The distinction matters: the unemployment rate only measures those who are available and actively searching.

How Is Unemployment Measured?

Two main methods are used in the UK. The Claimant Count adds up the number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits — specifically Jobseeker's Allowance and out-of-work Universal Credit claimants required to seek work. It is straightforward and published monthly, but it misses people who are unemployed yet not claiming benefits — for example, those who do not qualify.

The Labour Force Survey (LFS) is broader and more accurate. It interviews a large sample of households every three months and counts as unemployed anyone who is without work, available to start within two weeks, and has been actively seeking a job in the past four weeks. Because it uses a consistent international definition, the LFS figure is generally considered the more reliable measure.

Key Fact

The UK uses two main measures of unemployment: the Claimant Count (people claiming benefits) and the Labour Force Survey (a household survey using the international definition). The LFS is the broader and more widely used measure.

Types of Unemployment

Unemployment is not all the same. Economists identify four main types, each with a different cause. Understanding the type matters because it points to the right policy response.

Structural unemployment arises when industries decline and the skills of redundant workers do not match the vacancies that exist elsewhere in the economy. Coal miners made redundant when pits closed in the 1980s, or steelworkers displaced by cheaper imports, are classic examples. Because their skills are highly specific, it can take years to retrain and find new work. Structural unemployment tends to be long-term and concentrated in particular regions.

Cyclical unemployment is driven by the economic cycle. When the economy slows or enters a recession, consumer spending and business investment fall — firms cut back production and lay off workers. Cyclical unemployment therefore rises and falls with the business cycle: it grows during a downturn and shrinks during a recovery. It affects workers across many industries at the same time.

Frictional unemployment exists in every healthy economy. It describes the time a worker spends searching for a new job after leaving an old one — even in a booming labour market there are always some people between positions. Frictional unemployment tends to be brief and voluntary in nature.

Seasonal unemployment follows a predictable annual pattern. Agricultural workers, ski instructors and workers in the tourism and hospitality industries often face lower demand outside the peak season. In the UK, unemployment figures tend to rise slightly in winter when seasonal roles in sectors such as tourism and agriculture dry up.

Key Fact

The four main types of unemployment are: structural (skills mismatch from industrial decline), cyclical (falling demand during a recession), frictional (between jobs, short-term) and seasonal (predictable pattern linked to time of year).

Full Employment

Economists do not expect unemployment ever to reach zero. Even in a thriving economy there will always be some frictional unemployment — workers moving between jobs — and some seasonal variation. Full employment therefore means that cyclical and structural unemployment have been brought to very low levels, and only unavoidable frictional unemployment (workers between jobs) remains. When the government sets reducing unemployment as an objective, it is aiming for full employment in this sense.

The Consequences of Unemployment

Unemployment is harmful to many groups at the same time. Consider what happens when a car manufacturing plant in a town closes and hundreds of workers lose their jobs.

For the individual, the immediate impact is a loss of income. If the worker cannot quickly find alternative employment, their spending falls, their savings may be depleted, and their mental health and self-esteem can deteriorate. Long spells without work make it harder to find new employment because skills become outdated and CVs develop gaps that employers notice.

For the wider economy, unemployment causes lost output: if workers are idle, the goods and services they could have produced are simply not made. The economy operates inside its productive potential — resources are wasted. Local businesses in the town lose customers as workers spend less, which can trigger further job losses in a negative multiplier effect. This illustrates a chain of reasoning: unemployment rises → household incomes fall → consumer spending falls → local businesses see lower revenues → some may make further redundancies → unemployment rises further.

For the government, the costs are significant. Tax revenues fall because unemployed people pay less income tax and spend less (reducing VAT receipts). At the same time, spending on unemployment benefits and other welfare payments rises. The combination pushes the government’s budget towards a deficit. High unemployment can also create social costs: increased crime, poorer health outcomes, and greater inequality between regions.
exam_tip_html: Exam questions on unemployment typically use the command word Explain or Analyse. For Explain questions, develop a chain: give the type of unemployment, state its cause, and say what effect it has. For Analyse questions, trace the knock-on effects in a connected chain — for example, how rising cyclical unemployment reduces consumer spending, lowers tax revenue and increases government borrowing. For Evaluate questions, a common error is simply listing consequences without weighing them. Show which effect is most significant and why — the size of the impact will depend on how long unemployment lasts and which type it is.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Unemployment is measured in two ways in the UK: the Claimant Count (benefit claimants) and the Labour Force Survey (household survey using the international definition). The LFS is the broader measure.
  • There are four main types of unemployment: structural (skills mismatch), cyclical (falling demand in a recession), frictional (between jobs) and seasonal (time-of-year pattern).
  • Unemployment harms individuals through lost income and reduced wellbeing, damages the economy through lost output and a negative multiplier effect, and costs the government through lower tax revenues and higher welfare spending.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct definition of frictional unemployment?
A) Unemployment caused by workers having the wrong skills for available jobs
B) Unemployment that rises and falls with the economic cycle
C) Short-term unemployment while a worker is searching for a new job
D) Unemployment that follows a predictable seasonal pattern
practice_questions.marks: C) Short-term unemployment while a worker is searching for a new job [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: In a town, a factory employing 500 workers closes in January. In the following month, 500 fewer jobs are recorded, but the unemployment figure rises by only 380. Calculate the number of workers who are likely to have become economically inactive rather than unemployed, and show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: 500 (jobs lost) minus 380 (recorded as unemployed) = 120; 1 mark for the correct answer of 120 workers who became economically inactive.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Labour Force Survey is considered a more accurate measure of unemployment than the Claimant Count.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid reason (e.g. the LFS uses the international definition and captures people who are unemployed but not claiming benefits); 1 mark for developing the point (e.g. some unemployed people do not qualify for benefits or choose not to claim, so they are excluded from the Claimant Count); 1 mark for a further development or consequence (e.g. this means the Claimant Count understates the true level of unemployment, making it a less reliable guide for government policy).

practice_questions.text: A steel-producing region has seen its last major plant close following competition from overseas producers. Many of the workers are over 50, have worked in steel all their lives, and live in an area with few other employers. Explain how this situation illustrates structural unemployment and its likely effects on the workers involved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying this as structural unemployment; 1 mark for explaining the cause (the steel industry has declined permanently due to international competition, creating a skills mismatch — workers' experience does not match available vacancies); 1 mark for one effect on workers (e.g. prolonged unemployment because their skills are highly specific and retraining takes time; income falls and savings may be depleted); 1 mark for a further developed effect (e.g. the concentration in one region means local businesses also suffer as spending falls, deepening the economic damage in the area).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a rise in cyclical unemployment during a recession affects the government's finances.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-connected chain of reasoning: recession leads to higher cyclical unemployment → workers lose income → income tax receipts fall → unemployed workers increase demand for Jobseeker's Allowance and other benefits → government spending on welfare rises → the combination of lower revenue and higher spending pushes the budget towards a deficit → the government may need to borrow more, increasing national debt. The response links multiple effects and considers the two-sided fiscal squeeze (revenue down AND spending up).

Secure (3–4 marks): A clear explanation with at least two linked effects — e.g. lower income tax revenue and higher benefit payments — with some development but the chain may stop short of the budget deficit or borrowing consequence.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies one or two relevant effects (e.g. the government pays more in benefits) with limited development.

Emerging (1 mark): A simple, undeveloped point linking unemployment to government spending.

practice_questions.text: 'Structural unemployment is more damaging to an economy than cyclical unemployment.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (structural more damaging):
- Structural unemployment tends to be long-term: displaced workers with outdated skills can remain unemployed for years, leading to a permanent loss of productive capacity and human capital.
- It is geographically concentrated — entire regions can be blighted, creating persistent deprivation and social problems that are costly to address.
- Retraining and re-skilling workers is expensive and takes time, so the damage accumulates. The government faces ongoing welfare spending without a quick fix.

Arguments against (cyclical can be more damaging in the short run):
- Cyclical unemployment can affect the whole economy simultaneously and very rapidly during a deep recession, causing a much larger total increase in unemployment than structural unemployment typically does.
- The negative multiplier effect of cyclical unemployment — falling spending leads to further job losses — can be severe and self-reinforcing.
- Governments have tools to tackle cyclical unemployment (such as lowering interest rates or increasing public spending) but these do not resolve structural problems.

Judgement: It depends on the scale of the recession versus the scale of the structural change. For a small economy experiencing rapid deindustrialisation, structural unemployment may be more persistently damaging. However, a severe recession causing mass cyclical unemployment across every sector can be more immediately destructive. The time horizon also matters: cyclical unemployment resolves when the economy recovers, whereas structural unemployment can become permanent if not addressed by supply-side policies.

Mastering (8–9 marks): Both sides developed with chains of reasoning; a supported judgement that uses 'it depends on' logic.
Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides addressed with some development; a conclusion present but may lack a clear basis.
Developing (3–4 marks): One side developed well or both sides noted briefly; limited conclusion.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple points on one side only; no conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of unemployment is caused by a fall in demand across the whole economy during a recession?
Why does the Labour Force Survey give a higher unemployment figure than the Claimant Count?
options: It includes people who are unemployed but not claiming benefits
It counts only people aged over 25
It adds economically inactive people to the total

knowledge_checks.q: People of working age who are neither in work nor actively seeking a job are described as economically _____.
Structural unemployment arises when workers' _____ no longer match the jobs available in the economy.
Match each type of unemployment to its cause:
right: Industrial decline leaving workers with outdated skills
A worker searching for a new job between positions
Demand for work falling at certain times of year

flashcard_questions.a: A measure of unemployment counting those claiming Jobseeker's Allowance or out-of-work Universal Credit claimants who are required to seek work.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Labour Force Survey (LFS)?
flashcard_questions.a: A quarterly household survey that measures unemployment using the international definition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between the Claimant Count and the LFS?
flashcard_questions.a: The LFS captures unemployed people not claiming benefits, giving a broader figure.
A permanent industrial decline that leaves workers with skills that no longer match available jobs.
A fall in aggregate demand during a recession, reducing the demand for workers.
Short-term unemployment while a worker searches for a new job.
Demand for workers falling at predictable times of year in sectors such as tourism or agriculture.

flashcard_questions.q: In economics, what does 'full employment' mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Cyclical and structural unemployment are minimal; only unavoidable frictional unemployment remains.
Working-age people who are neither employed nor actively seeking work.

flashcard_questions.q: How does rising unemployment affect government finances?
flashcard_questions.a: Tax revenues fall and welfare spending rises, pushing the budget towards a deficit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the negative multiplier effect of unemployment?
flashcard_questions.a: Falling incomes reduce consumer spending, causing further business revenue falls and more job losses.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is structural unemployment often long-lasting?
flashcard_questions.a: Retraining workers with highly specific outdated skills takes considerable time and investment.

glossary_terms.definition: The state of being in paid work — the proportion of working-age people who have a job.
The state of being without a job despite being willing and able to work and actively seeking employment.
People of working age who are neither employed nor actively seeking work, such as full-time students, carers or those who have given up job-searching.
A measure of unemployment counting those claiming Jobseeker's Allowance or out-of-work Universal Credit claimants required to seek work; published monthly.
A quarterly survey of approximately 27,000–30,000 households that measures employment and unemployment using the International Labour Organisation definition.
Unemployment caused by a permanent shift in the structure of the economy, so that workers' skills no longer match the jobs available.
Unemployment caused by a fall in the overall level of demand in the economy, typically during a recession.
Short-term unemployment that occurs when workers are in between jobs and searching for a new position.
Unemployment that follows a predictable pattern related to the time of year, affecting industries whose demand is concentrated in certain seasons.
An economic situation in which everyone who wants a job and is able to work can find one, although a small amount of frictional unemployment always remains.
The maximum possible output an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.
